claim: Twelve patients with chronic left temporal stroke and 12 matched controls were mapped and tested using auditory temporal order and discrimination tasks.
source: Twelve patients with chronic left temporal stroke and 12 matched controls (Supplementary file 1) were mapped and tested using auditory temporal order and discrimination tasks (same-different judgments).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of participants and the tasks used in the study.

claim: Patients with left temporal stroke showed higher temporal order thresholds compared to controls.
source: In contrast, patients required longer intervals to judge the order of two different frequency tones (U = 114, p = 0.007, effect size r = 0.495; Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Statistical test results (Mann-Whitney U test) and reference to Figure 2A provide empirical support.

claim: Patients with left temporal stroke showed higher micropattern discrimination thresholds compared to controls.
source: In contrast, patients required longer intervals to judge the order of two different frequency tones (U = 114, p = 0.007, effect size r = 0.495; Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1) and to discriminate two micropatterns (U = 120.5, p = 0.002, r = 0.572; Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statistical test results and reference to Figure 2B provide empirical support.

claim: Order and discrimination thresholds were positively correlated in patients.
source: Order and discrimination thresholds were positively correlated in patients (p = 0.015, Spearman's rho rs = 0.681)
evidence: Correlation analysis with statistical significance is reported.

claim: Order and discrimination thresholds were positively correlated in controls.
source: Order and discrimination thresholds were positively correlated in patients (p = 0.015, Spearman's rho rs = 0.681) and controls (p = 0.006, rs = 0.735).
evidence: Correlation analysis with statistical significance is reported.

claim: Error rates differed in patients and controls for the discrimination of words, pseudowords, and phonemes.
source: Error rates differed in patients and controls for the discrimination of words, pseudowords, and phonemes (Friedman test, χ2(2) = 16.026, p = 0.0002).
evidence: Statistical test results (Friedman test) demonstrate significant differences.

claim: Phoneme discrimination displayed increased error rates compared to words in patients and controls combined.
source: Phoneme discrimination displayed increased error rates compared to words (Z = –3.624, p = 0.0003, r = 0.740, Bonferroni adjustment at p < 0.017)
evidence: Post-hoc statistical test results with Bonferroni correction are provided.

claim: Pseudoword discrimination displayed increased error rates compared to words in patients and controls combined.
source: Phoneme discrimination displayed increased error rates compared to words (Z = –3.624, p = 0.0003, r = 0.740, Bonferroni adjustment at p < 0.017) and pseudowords compared to words (Z = –2.684, p = 0.007, r = 0.548).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical test results with Bonferroni correction are provided.

claim: Patients showed higher error rates for phonemes than words.
source: Although healthy controls did not show any category effect, patients (χ2(2) = 10.857, p = 0.003) showed higher error rates for phonemes than words (Z = –2.287, p = 0.015, r = 0.660)
evidence: Statistical test results specific to the patient group are reported.

claim: Patients showed higher error rates for pseudowords than words.
source: Although healthy controls did not show any category effect, patients (χ2(2) = 10.857, p = 0.003) showed higher error rates for phonemes than words (Z = –2.287, p = 0.015, r = 0.660), and for pseudowords than words (Z = –2.666, p = 0.002, r = 0.769).
evidence: Statistical test results specific to the patient group are reported.

claim: Patients with left posterior temporal strokes show less accurate auditory spectro-temporal processing and concomitant perceptual speech deficits.
source: Thus, in line with previous results (Chedru et al., 1978; Efron, 1963; Swisher and Hirsh, 1972), we confirm that patients with left posterior temporal strokes show less accurate auditory spectro-temporal processing and concomitant perceptual speech deficits.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented and cited previous research.

claim: Patients showed significant effects for contrastive features for phoneme pairs.
source: Only patients showed significant effects for contrastive features for phoneme (χ2(2) = 18.313, p = 0.00004) and pseudoword pairs (Z = –2.38, p = 0.008, r = 0.687).
evidence: Statistical test results demonstrate significant effects in patients.

claim: Patients showed significant effects for contrastive features for pseudoword pairs.
source: Only patients showed significant effects for contrastive features for phoneme (χ2(2) = 18.313, p = 0.00004) and pseudoword pairs (Z = –2.38, p = 0.008, r = 0.687).
evidence: Statistical test results demonstrate significant effects in patients.

claim: Patients showed higher error rates for the discrimination of place of articulation contrasts than for voicing in phonemes.
source: Post hoc Wilcoxon tests (Bonferroni-adjusted significance level at p < 0.0083) confirmed higher error rates for the discrimination of place of articulation contrasts than for voicing (Z = −2.521, p = 0.004, r = 0.728) in phonemes.
evidence: Post-hoc statistical test results with Bonferroni correction are provided.

claim: Patients showed higher error rates for place of articulation compared to combined place of articulation and voicing contrast in phonemes.
source: The same was true when comparing place of articulation to combined place of articulation and voicing contrast (Z = −2.536, p = 0.004, r = 0.732)
evidence: Post-hoc statistical test results are provided.

claim: Patients showed higher error rates for place of articulation compared to fricative contrasts in phonemes.
source: The same was true when comparing place of articulation to combined place of articulation and voicing contrast (Z = −2.536, p = 0.004, r = 0.732) as well as for place of articulation compared to fricative contrasts (Z = −2.555, p = 0.004, r = 0.738).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical test results are provided.

claim: Patients showed higher error rates for place of articulation relative to manner of articulation contrasts in pseudowords.
source: Similarly, patients showed higher error rates for place of articulation relative to manner of articulation contrasts (Z = –2.684, p = 0.004, r = 0.775) in pseudowords.
evidence: Statistical test results are provided.

claim: Patients displayed higher error rates for the discrimination of place of articulation contrasts in pseudowords compared to controls.
source: Subsequent between-group comparisons revealed higher error rates for the discrimination of place of articulation contrasts in pseudowords in patients but not controls (U = 101.5, p = 0.045, r = 0.348)
evidence: Between-group statistical comparison is reported.

claim: Patients displayed speech processing deficits preeminent for information encoded in the spectro-temporal fine structure at short timescales.
source: In sum, patients displayed speech processing deficits preeminent for information encoded in the spectro-temporal fine structure at short timescales (Rosen, 1992).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented and cited research.

claim: There was a positive correlation between error rates for voicing contrasts in phoneme discrimination with threshold levels for auditory order.
source: There was a positive correlation between error rates for voicing contrasts in phoneme discrimination with threshold levels for auditory order (p = 0.032, r = 0.549)
evidence: Correlation analysis with statistical significance is reported.

claim: There was a positive correlation between error rates for voicing contrasts in phoneme discrimination with threshold levels for micropattern discrimination.
source: There was a positive correlation between error rates for voicing contrasts in phoneme discrimination with threshold levels for auditory order (p = 0.032, r = 0.549) and micropattern discrimination (p = 0.043, r = 0.516).
evidence: Correlation analysis with statistical significance is reported.

claim: No significant associations were found between lesion volume and threshold values or error rates for feature discrimination.
source: Importantly, no significant associations were found between lesion volume or hearing loss and threshold values or error rates for feature discrimination (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of significant associations.

claim: No significant associations were found between hearing loss and threshold values or error rates for feature discrimination.
source: Importantly, no significant associations were found between lesion volume or hearing loss and threshold values or error rates for feature discrimination (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of significant associations.

claim: Patients exhibit a short timescale specific perceptual deficit for tones and phonemes.
source: In line with our hypotheses and previous findings (Fink et al., 2006; Robson et al., 2013), we show that patients exhibit a short timescale specific perceptual deficit for tones and phonemes.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented and cited previous research.

claim: Six patients showed impaired performance in at least two subtests (deficit-positive lesion group, LG+).
source: This procedure effectively split the patient group into two sub-groups of equal size, as six patients showed impaired performance in at least two subtests (deficit-positive lesion group, LG+) as compared to six patients (deficit-negative lesion group, LG−) performing similarly to controls (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the grouping procedure and references Figure 2C-D.

claim: Six patients performed similarly to controls (deficit-negative lesion group, LG−).
source: This procedure effectively split the patient group into two sub-groups of equal size, as six patients showed impaired performance in at least two subtests (deficit-positive lesion group, LG+) as compared to six patients (deficit-negative lesion group, LG−) performing similarly to controls (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the grouping procedure and references Figure 2C-D.

claim: The patient groups (LG+ and LG−) did not differ in terms of demographic or clinical characteristics.
source: The patient groups did not differ in terms of demographic or clinical characteristics (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of differences and references supplementary data.

claim: The maximal lesion overlap was centered on the posterior superior surface of the left superior temporal gyrus (planum temporale) extending into the underlying white matter.
source: The maximal lesion overlap (Figure 1A) was centered on the posterior superior surface of the left superior temporal gyrus (STG) (planum temporale) extending into the underlying white matter.
evidence: The manuscript describes the lesion overlap location and references Figure 1A.

claim: The lesion subtraction of LG− patients from LG+ patients linked pSTS, adjacent middle temporal gyrus (MTG), and white matter below the STS to the spectro-temporal encoding impairment in the LG+ group.
source: In contrast, the lesion subtraction of LG− patients from LG+ patients (Figure 3A) linked pSTS, adjacent middle temporal gyrus (MTG), and white matter below the STS to the spectro-temporal encoding impairment in the LG+ group.
evidence: The manuscript describes the lesion subtraction analysis and references Figure 3A.

claim: Differences in lesion distribution between LG− and LG+ patients were statistically confirmed.
source: Differences in lesion distribution between LG− and LG+patients were statistically confirmed (Liebermeister test, binomial data with 1 = LG+ and 0 = LG−, permutation FWE-corrected α-level of p < 0.05) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical test results and reference to Figure 3B are provided.

claim: Long association and projection fibers originating from the seed masks in the pSTS and the subjacent white matter below the STS were identified within the anterior floor of the left external capsule, the left periventricular white matter, and the brain stem.
source: Long association and projection fibers originating from the seed masks in the pSTS and the subjacent white matter below the STS (Figure 3B) were identified within the anterior floor of the left external capsule, the left periventricular white matter, and the brain stem.
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results and references Figure 3B.

claim: Connectivity was indicated along the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) traveling within the anterior floor of the external capsule with terminations in the left inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis, BA 45) and in the lateral orbitofrontal cortex (BA 47).
source: Subdivision into separate fiber bundles (Figure 4) indicated connectivity along the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) traveling within the anterior floor of the external capsule. Terminations were present in the left inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis, Brodmann area [BA] 45) and in the lateral orbitofrontal cortex (BA 47).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results and references Figure 4.

claim: Association fibers extended along the posterior lateral surface of the lateral ventricle to the left superior parietal cortex (BA 7).
source: Association fibers also extended along the posterior lateral surface of the lateral ventricle to the left superior parietal cortex (BA 7).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results.

claim: Association fibers extending to the superior parietal cortex may correspond to the posterior middle longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).
source: Considering the characteristic connectivity patterns of these association fibers with the superior parietal cortex, they may correspond to the posterior middle longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) (Makris et al., 2013a; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript infers the identity of the fiber tract based on connectivity patterns and cites supporting literature.

claim: Cortico-cortical association fibers traveled rostrally within the periventricular white matter lateral to the corona radiata in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) with terminations in the left inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis, BA 44) and the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (BA 9, BA 46).
source: Other cortico-cortical association fibers curved upward and traveled rostrally within the periventricular white matter lateral to the corona radiata in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) with terminations in the left inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis, BA 44) and the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (BA 9, BA 46).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results.

claim: Fibers originating in the superior posterior temporal cortex reached the posterolateral cerebellum (crura I and II) and the dentate nuclei bilaterally.
source: Most importantly, fibers originating in the superior posterior temporal cortex (Figure 5A) reached the posterolateral cerebellum (crura I and II) and the dentate nuclei bilaterally (Figure 4 and Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results and references Figures 4, 5A, and 5B.

claim: Fibers from the superior posterior temporal cortex coursed rostrally and ascended medially near the posterior temporal and inferior parietal cortex before they descended through the retrolenticular internal capsule along the left cerebral peduncle to the pontine nuclei and the ipsilateral middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP).
source: These fibers coursed rostrally and ascended medially near the posterior temporal and inferior parietal cortex before they descended through the retrolenticular internal capsule along the left cerebral peduncle to the pontine nuclei and the ipsilateral middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP).
evidence: The manuscript describes the trajectory of fibers identified through tractography.

claim: Fibers from the superior posterior temporal cortex decussated at the ventral pons to the right cerebellar peduncle, giving rise to bilateral temporo-ponto-cerebellar tracts.
source: They additionally decussated at the ventral pons to the right cerebellar peduncle, giving rise to bilateral temporo-ponto-cerebellar tracts (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results and references Figure 5B.

claim: Fibers conformed to the cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract connecting the posterior superior temporal cortex with the bilateral dentate nuclei along the superior cerebellar peduncles (SCPs).
source: Other fibers conformed to the cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract connecting the posterior superior temporal cortex with the bilateral dentate nuclei along the superior cerebellar peduncles (SCPs).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results.

claim: Fibers of the cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract crossed at the level of the inferior olive to the left red nucleus and projected to the posterior thalamus (pulvinar).
source: They crossed at the level of the inferior olive to the left red nucleus and projected to the posterior thalamus (pulvinar) (Figures 4 and 5B).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results and references Figures 4 and 5B.

claim: Lesions in the left pSTS led to a spectro-temporal processing deficit at short timescales for lower-level auditory and speech information.
source: Taken together, the results demonstrate that lesions in the left pSTS led to a spectro-temporal processing deficit at short timescales for lower-level auditory and speech information.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating the lesion and behavioral findings.

claim: A bidirectional temporo-cerebellar connectivity was confirmed by probabilistic tractography.
source: The neural substrate for such perceptual necessities is revealed here for the first time: a bidirectional temporo-cerebellar connectivity confirmed by probabilistic tractography.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the tractography findings.

claim: Tractography from control seed regions in the left IPL, AG, and pMTG showed no relevant cortico-cerebellar connectivity along the MCP and SCP.
source: Tractography from these control seed regions however showed no relevant cortico-cerebellar connectivity along the MCP and SCP.
evidence: The manuscript describes control analysis results.

claim: The absence of cortico-cerebellar connectivity from control regions supports the specificity of the reported temporo-cerebellar tracts originating from the STS in the context of impaired processing of sound at short timescales.
source: This supports the specificity of the reported temporo-cerebellar tracts originating from the STS in the context of impaired processing of sound at short timescales.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control analysis results.

claim: Tractography from the foot area of the motor cortex revealed bilateral connectivity along the pyramidal tract with terminations in cerebellar lobulus VIII.
source: Tractography from the second control seed region in the foot area of the motor cortex revealed bilateral connectivity along the pyramidal tract with terminations in cerebellar lobulus VIII (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) that corresponds to regions associated with motor processing (i.e., the motor cerebellum) (Stoodley et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript describes control analysis results and references Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and a citation.

claim: Cerebellar lobulus VIII corresponds to regions associated with motor processing (i.e., the motor cerebellum).
source: Tractography from the second control seed region in the foot area of the motor cortex revealed bilateral connectivity along the pyramidal tract with terminations in cerebellar lobulus VIII (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) that corresponds to regions associated with motor processing (i.e., the motor cerebellum) (Stoodley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Different projections in the thalamus were found, where fibers to the motor cortex could be delineated in the ventral lateral thalamic nuclei and fibers to the temporal cortex in the posterior thalamus.
source: In contrast, we found different projections in the thalamus, where fibers to the motor cortex could be delineated in the ventral lateral thalamic nuclei and fibers to the temporal cortex in the posterior thalamus (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes tractography results and references Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The control analysis results demonstrate the specificity of temporo-cerebellar and thalamo-temporal projections in relation to impaired processing of sound at short timescales.
source: These results further demonstrate the specificity of temporo-cerebellar and thalamo-temporal projections in relation to impaired processing of sound at short timescales.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the control analysis findings.

claim: The cerebellum plays a foundational role in monitoring motor performance and its sensory consequences.
source: Current theories of motor control postulate that the cerebellum plays a foundational role in monitoring motor performance and its sensory consequences (Wolpert et al., 1995; Wolpert and Miall, 1996).
evidence: This is stated based on cited theories.

claim: The cerebellar concept has been extended to anticipatory sensory and cognitive processes.
source: This important concept has been extended to anticipatory sensory and cognitive processes (Ito, 2008; Ramnani, 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Cortico-cerebellar interfaces implement essential properties of motor and non-motor (internal) models.
source: In this view, cortico-cerebellar interfaces implement essential properties of motor and non-motor (internal) models, that is, representations that can be used to anticipate future events, thereby maximizing the precision of motor, sensory, and cognitive performance (Ito, 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The cerebellar timing hypothesis claims that the cerebellum encodes the precise temporal locus of sensory events.
source: The cerebellar timing hypothesis claims that the cerebellum encodes the precise temporal locus of sensory events (Ivry et al., 2002; Spencer and Ivry, 2013), with potential asymmetric hemispheric sensitivities.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The right cerebellar hemisphere prefers rapid signal modulations while the left prefers slow signal modulations.
source: While the right cerebellar hemisphere prefers rapid, the left prefers slow signal modulations (Callan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The sampling of continuous sounds has been argued to proceed in time windows of different lengths, which translate into different linguistic segments of speech.
source: Concretely, the sampling of continuous sounds has been argued to proceed in time windows of different lengths, which, in turn, translate into different linguistic segments of speech (e.g., phonemes and syllables) (Flinker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Damage to the cerebellum impairs the perception of temporal voicing contrasts.
source: Existing deficit lesion data show that damage to the cerebellum impairs the perception of temporal voicing contrasts (Ackermann et al., 1997)
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Damage to the cerebellum impairs duration judgments of intervals.
source: Existing deficit lesion data show that damage to the cerebellum impairs the perception of temporal voicing contrasts (Ackermann et al., 1997), duration judgments of intervals (Ivry and Keele, 1989)
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Damage to the cerebellum impairs the ability to use temporal event structure to update a representation of the auditory environment.
source: Existing deficit lesion data show that damage to the cerebellum impairs the perception of temporal voicing contrasts (Ackermann et al., 1997), duration judgments of intervals (Ivry and Keele, 1989), and the ability to use temporal event structure to update a representation of the auditory environment (Kotz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Left temporal cortex lesions lead to impairments of temporal order judgments.
source: Similarly, left temporal cortex lesions, in particular, lead to impairments of temporal order judgments (Efron, 1963; Swisher and Hirsh, 1972)
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Left temporal cortex lesions lead to discrimination impairments of rapidly presented complex tone pairs (micropatterns).
source: Similarly, left temporal cortex lesions, in particular, lead to impairments of temporal order judgments (Efron, 1963; Swisher and Hirsh, 1972), discrimination of rapidly presented complex tone pairs (micropatterns; Chedru et al., 1978)
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Left temporal cortex lesions lead to phonological discrimination impairments associated with increased detection thresholds for rapid (but not slow) modulations.
source: Similarly, left temporal cortex lesions, in particular, lead to impairments of temporal order judgments (Efron, 1963; Swisher and Hirsh, 1972), discrimination of rapidly presented complex tone pairs (micropatterns; Chedru et al., 1978), phonological discrimination associated with increased detection thresholds for rapid (but not slow) modulations (Robson et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Left temporal cortex lesions lead to impaired detection of short timescale voicing contrasts and increased temporal order thresholds.
source: Similarly, left temporal cortex lesions, in particular, lead to impairments of temporal order judgments (Efron, 1963; Swisher and Hirsh, 1972), discrimination of rapidly presented complex tone pairs (micropatterns; Chedru et al., 1978), phonological discrimination associated with increased detection thresholds for rapid (but not slow) modulations (Robson et al., 2013), detection of short timescale voicing contrasts, and increased temporal order thresholds (Fink et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Patients with left posterior superior temporal sulcus stroke are expected to show impaired temporal discrimination for non-verbal and verbal information, restricted to fast modulations.
source: Based on an extensive literature, such patients are expected to show impaired temporal discrimination for non-verbal and verbal information, restricted to fast modulations, such as voicing and place of articulation contrasts Boemio et al., 2005; Elangovan and Stuart, 2008; Rosen, 1992).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited literature.

claim: Specific lesion-symptom mapping will identify a critical seed region to distinguish the well-documented dorsal and ventral fiber tracts of the temporo-frontal speech network.
source: Second, we predict that specific lesion-symptom mapping will identify a critical seed region to distinguish the well-documented dorsal and ventral fiber tracts of the temporo-frontal speech network (Frey et al., 2008; Friederici, 2011; Saur et al., 2008; Turken and Dronkers, 2011).
evidence: This is a prediction based on cited literature.

claim: Anatomic tractography should reveal direct connections linking the left posterior temporal cortex with the right posterior lateral cerebellum (cerebellar crura I/II).
source: Third, and most critically, if the generalized timing conjecture is on the right track, anatomic tractrography should reveal direct connections linking the left posterior temporal cortex with the right posterior lateral cerebellum (cerebellar crura I/II), ostensibly engaged in auditory processing (Petacchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the timing conjecture and cited literature.

claim: Behavioral deficits can be explained similarly by local brain damage and indirectly measured disconnection.
source: In this regard, it was shown that behavioral deficits can be explained similarly by local brain damage and indirectly measured disconnection (Salvalaggio et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Healthy controls showed typical threshold values comparable to previously reported temporal order (SOAs above 15–60 ms) and micropattern discrimination tasks (SOAs of at least of 5 ms).
source: Healthy controls showed typical threshold values comparable to previously reported temporal order (SOAs above 15–60 ms) and micropattern discrimination tasks (SOAs of at least of 5 ms) (Efron, 1963; Efron, 1973; Hirsh and Sherrick, 1961; Yund and Efron, 1974).
evidence: This is stated based on data and cited literature.

claim: The term 'micropattern' describes pairs of complex tones presented with stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs) below an individual's temporal order threshold.
source: The term 'micropattern' describes pairs of complex tones presented with stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs) below an individual's temporal order threshold, that is, the shortest SOA at which the temporal order of two tones can be perceived (Chedru et al., 1978; Anstis et al., 1978).
evidence: This is a definition based on cited literature.

claim: Frequency reversals within a micropattern lead to a perceptual dissociation where micropatterns are perceived as relatively lower or higher in pitch.
source: However, frequency reversals within a micropattern lead to a perceptual dissociation. Micropatterns are perceived as relatively lower or higher in pitch, a phenomenon attributed to the perceptual dominance of the second stimulus frequency (Efron, 1973).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The place of articulation contrast is likely represented in the spectro-temporal fine structure occurring over short timescales (20–50 ms).
source: This feature is likely represented in the spectro-temporal fine structure occurring over short timescales (20–50 ms), whereas phonemic contrasts to voicing and manner are encoded in timescale duration differences of voice-onset times (Elangovan and Stuart, 2008) and the slowly varying temporal envelope (50–500 ms; Rosen, 1992).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Phonemic contrasts to voicing and manner are encoded in timescale duration differences of voice-onset times and the slowly varying temporal envelope (50–500 ms).
source: This feature is likely represented in the spectro-temporal fine structure occurring over short timescales (20–50 ms), whereas phonemic contrasts to voicing and manner are encoded in timescale duration differences of voice-onset times (Elangovan and Stuart, 2008) and the slowly varying temporal envelope (50–500 ms; Rosen, 1992).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Discrimination thresholds and discrimination performance for non-verbal and verbal information go hand in hand, suggesting a common process that contributes to short timescale spectro-temporal encoding.
source: In contrast to earlier findings (Chedru et al., 1978), we show that discrimination thresholds and discrimination performance for non-verbal and verbal information go hand in hand. This suggests a common process that contributes to short timescale spectro-temporal encoding for both non-verbal and verbal information
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data and contrasted with cited literature.

claim: Impaired auditory temporal processing can (at least partly) explain lower-level auditory deficits cascading into speech comprehension deficits.
source: This suggests a common process that contributes to short timescale spectro-temporal encoding for both non-verbal and verbal information – and that impaired auditory temporal processing can (at least partly) explain lower-level auditory deficits cascading into speech comprehension deficits (Robson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by data and cited literature.

claim: Higher-order auditory areas in the superior temporal cortices preferentially encode rapidly changing auditory signals in time windows of ~20–40 ms in the left hemisphere and of ~150–250 ms in the right hemisphere.
source: These are thought to preferentially encode rapidly changing auditory signals in time windows of ~20–40 ms in the left hemisphere and of ~150–250 ms in the right hemisphere (Boemio et al., 2005; Flinker et al., 2019; Poeppel, 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Tractography findings of cortico-cortical structural connectivity are in line with results mapping speech processing networks that connect to the left MTG/STS along the IFOF and the SLF with BA 47 and BA 46.
source: Our tractography findings of cortico-cortical structural connectivity are in line with results mapping speech processing networks that connect to the left MTG/STS along the IFOF and the SLF with BA 47 and BA 46 (Turken and Dronkers, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with cited literature.

claim: Functionally distinct subdivisions of the SLF, namely the SLF III and arcuate fasciculus, may provide higher-order (somato-)sensory and auditory input to inferior frontal (BA 44) or dorsolateral prefrontal regions (BA 46, BA 6/8).
source: Functionally distinct subdivisions of the SLF, namely the SLF III and arcuate fasciculus, may provide higher-order (somato-)sensory and auditory input to inferior frontal (BA 44) or dorsolateral prefrontal regions (BA 46, BA 6/8; Makris et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Studies revealed connectivity along the middle longitudinal fascicle between the posterior temporal cortex and the superior parietal lobe (BA 7), an area associated with audio-visual multisensory integration.
source: Other studies revealed connectivity along the middle longitudinal fascicle between the posterior temporal cortex and the superior parietal lobe (BA 7; Makris et al., 2013b; Wang et al., 2013), an area associated with audio-visual multisensory integration (Molholm et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Cerebellar contributions to higher cognitive functions have been related to reciprocal prefrontal-cerebellar and posterior parieto-cerebellar projections, connecting association cortices with the lateral and posterior cerebellar hemispheres.
source: To date, such contributions have been related to reciprocal prefrontal-cerebellar and posterior parieto-cerebellar projections, connecting association cortices with the lateral and posterior cerebellar hemispheres (Brodal, 1978b; Brodal, 1978a; Brodal, 1979; Jissendi et al., 2008; Kelly and Strick, 2003; Ramnani et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Earlier claims considering temporo-cerebellar projections based on diffusion-weighted imaging of the cerebral peduncles as insignificant in both humans and non-human primates should be revised.
source: Earlier claims considering temporo-cerebellar projections based on diffusion-weighted imaging of the cerebral peduncles as insignificant in both humans and non-human primates (Ramnani et al., 2006) should be revised
evidence: This is a statement challenging cited literature based on the current findings.

claim: The topographical distribution of cortico-ponto-cerebellar projections likely extends beyond and is distinct from the most prominent prefrontal and primary motor structural connectivity patterns.
source: Earlier claims considering temporo-cerebellar projections based on diffusion-weighted imaging of the cerebral peduncles as insignificant in both humans and non-human primates (Ramnani et al., 2006) should be revised, as the topographical distribution of cortico-ponto-cerebellar projections likely extends beyond and is distinct from the most prominent prefrontal and primary motor structural connectivity patterns (see Results – Control analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and references to control analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cortico-cerebellar system may comprise reciprocal ipsi- and contralateral temporo-cerebellar projections that have gained very little attention.
source: As demonstrated here, the cortico-cerebellar system may also comprise reciprocal ipsi- and contralateral temporo-cerebellar projections that so far have gained only very little attention (Schmahmann and Pandya, 2009; Schmahmann and Pandya, 1991; Sokolov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: The present findings confirm fibers connecting the superior posterior temporal cortex and the posterior lateral cerebellum (crura I/II, cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract).
source: Moreover, the present findings confirm fibers connecting the superior posterior temporal cortex and the posterior lateral cerebellum (crura I/II, cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract)
evidence: This is a summary statement of the tractography findings.

claim: The present findings indicate fibers originating in bilateral dentate nuclei, which run along the SCP and posterior thalamus (cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract).
source: Moreover, the present findings confirm fibers connecting the superior posterior temporal cortex and the posterior lateral cerebellum (crura I/II, cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract) and indicate fibers originating in bilateral dentate nuclei, which run along the SCP and posterior thalamus (cerebello-rubro-thalamic tract).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the tractography findings.

claim: These observations confirm the concept of reciprocal cortico-cerebello-cortical loops.
source: These observations confirm the concept of reciprocal cortico-cerebello-cortical loops (Salmi et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: The findings conform to anatomical landmarks for cerebro-cerebellar connections in the brain stem and thalamus demonstrated in previous neuroanatomical and MRI studies.
source: These observations confirm the concept of reciprocal cortico-cerebello-cortical loops (Salmi et al., 2010) and conform to anatomical landmarks for cerebro-cerebellar connections in the brain stem and thalamus demonstrated in previous neuroanatomical and MRI studies (Bernard et al., 2014; Brodal, 1978b; Brodal, 1979; Dum and Strick, 2003; Habas and Cabanis, 2006; Habas and Cabanis, 2007; Pandya et al., 1994; Schmahmann and Pandya, 1991).
evidence: This is stated based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: There is bilateral posterior lateral cerebellar contributions to auditory processing.
source: In contrast to the bilateral posterior lateral cerebellar contributions to auditory (Pastor et al., 2002; Petacchi et al., 2005) and temporal processing (Ivry et al., 2002; Keele and Ivry, 1990; Spencer and Ivry, 2013), there is sparse evidence on temporo-cerebellar coupling (Pastor et al., 2002; Pastor et al., 2006b; Pastor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: There is bilateral posterior lateral cerebellar contributions to temporal processing.
source: In contrast to the bilateral posterior lateral cerebellar contributions to auditory (Pastor et al., 2002; Petacchi et al., 2005) and temporal processing (Ivry et al., 2002; Keele and Ivry, 1990; Spencer and Ivry, 2013), there is sparse evidence on temporo-cerebellar coupling (Pastor et al., 2002; Pastor et al., 2006b; Pastor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: There is sparse evidence on temporo-cerebellar coupling.
source: In contrast to the bilateral posterior lateral cerebellar contributions to auditory (Pastor et al., 2002; Petacchi et al., 2005) and temporal processing (Ivry et al., 2002; Keele and Ivry, 1990; Spencer and Ivry, 2013), there is sparse evidence on temporo-cerebellar coupling (Pastor et al., 2002; Pastor et al., 2006b; Pastor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Temporo-cerebellar coupling may support the continuous updating of internal models of the auditory environment.
source: However, such coupling may support the continuous updating of internal models of the auditory environment (Kotz et al., 2014) based on precise encoding of temporal structure.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Functional imaging studies show increased induced oscillatory activity in response to 40 Hz auditory stimulation in the bilateral posterolateral cerebellum (crus II).
source: For example, functional imaging studies show increased induced oscillatory activity in response to 40 Hz auditory stimulation (corresponding to a sampling period of ~25 ms) in the bilateral posterolateral cerebellum (crus II) (Pastor et al., 2002)
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Effective connectivity between superior temporal areas (STG and STS) and cerebellar crus II increases with 40 Hz auditory stimulation.
source: For example, functional imaging studies show increased induced oscillatory activity in response to 40 Hz auditory stimulation (corresponding to a sampling period of ~25 ms) in the bilateral posterolateral cerebellum (crus II) (Pastor et al., 2002), and effective connectivity between superior temporal areas (STG and STS) and cerebellar crus II increases with 40 Hz auditory stimulation (Pastor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Cortical oscillatory responses to 40 Hz auditory stimulation diminish after inhibitory cerebellar transcranial magnetic stimulation.
source: Likewise, cortical oscillatory responses to 40 Hz auditory stimulation diminish after inhibitory cerebellar transcranial magnetic stimulation (Pastor et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Induced gamma band oscillatory activity in the auditory cortex as well as in the cerebellum in response to random auditory stimulation tightly time-locks to auditory stimulus onsets.
source: Moreover, induced gamma band oscillatory activity in the auditory cortex as well as in the cerebellum in response to random auditory stimulation tightly time-locks to auditory stimulus onsets (Demiralp and Basar-Eroglu, 1996).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The cerebellum likely supports the encoding of an event-based representation of the temporal structure extracted from the auditory input signal by tracking salient modulations.
source: The cerebellum likely supports the encoding of an event-based representation of the temporal structure extracted from the auditory input signal by tracking salient modulations (e.g., changing sound energy levels as in onset transients or frequency transitions) of the physical sound across time that contribute to the segmentation of a continuous auditory input signal into smaller perceptual units.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Reciprocal temporo-cerebellar interactions might provide a unitary stimulus representation at different timescales for later processing stages.
source: Such reciprocal temporo-cerebellar interactions might provide a unitary stimulus representation at different timescales for later processing stages (Schwartze and Kotz, 2016; Schwartze et al., 2012; Weise et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: A temporally structured event representation may map the detailed cortical representation of auditory sensory information to relevant points in time, allowing for salient sound features to be optimally processed.
source: The overlap with the encoding of auditory signals in temporal integration windows of different lengths (Boemio et al., 2005) and possible cerebellar encoding of event boundaries across different timescales (Callan et al., 2007) suggests that a temporally structured event representation may map the detailed cortical representation of auditory sensory information to relevant points in time (Figure 6), allowing for salient sound features to be optimally processed (Kotz and Schwartze, 2010; Schwartze and Kotz, 2013; Schwartze and Kotz, 2016; Schwartze et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on cited literature and references Figure 6.

claim: The bilateral STS receive input differently from the STG through intra- and interhemispheric fibers, weighting information toward short timescales of sound processing.
source: In this regard, Boemio et al., 2005 showed in an fMRI study that the STS but not the STG shows duration-sensitive lateralization for shorter and longer timescales. Based on these findings the authors proposed that the bilateral STS receive input differently from the STG through intra- and interhemispheric fibers, weighting information toward short timescales of sound processing.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Weighting of information toward short timescales might be guided by event boundaries across different timescales encoded in both cerebellar hemispheres.
source: Such weighting might be guided by event boundaries across different timescales encoded in both cerebellar hemispheres.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings.

claim: The prefrontal cortex (supplementary motor area, BA 6) and its connections to the cerebellum play an essential role in the temporal integration of sensory information in auditory processing.
source: Notably, in auditory processing the prefrontal cortex (supplementary motor area, BA 6; Pastor et al., 2006a) and its connections to the cerebellum (Aso et al., 2010; Jissendi et al., 2008) play an essential role in the temporal integration of sensory information (Schwartze and Kotz, 2013; Schwartze et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: An extended network, consisting of prefrontal cortex, temporal cortex, and cerebellum, provides a platform to integrate sensory input over different timescales to continuously update spectro-temporal models of the auditory environment, thus optimizing sound processing.
source: This extended network, consisting of prefrontal cortex, temporal cortex, and cerebellum, provides a platform to integrate sensory input over different timescales to continuously update spectro-temporal models of the auditory environment, thus optimizing sound processing (Kotz and Schwartze, 2010; Kotz et al., 2014; Schwartze and Kotz, 2013; Schwartze et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: The illustrated cortico-subcortical and cortico-cortical structural connectivity pattern is presumably not unique for auditory temporal processing but showcases one possible general role for perceptual processing.
source: Many investigations have put forward theories on the cerebellum's role in perception and cognition (for a review, see Baumann et al., 2015), and the illustrated cortico-subcortical and cortico-cortical structural connectivity pattern is presumably not unique for auditory temporal processing but showcases one possible general role for perceptual processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: The study population is relatively small and lesion-symptom mapping is typically applied to larger populations with wider lesion distribution.
source: First, the study population is relatively small and lesion-symptom mapping is typically applied to larger populations with wider lesion distribution.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: It is possible that additional regions are involved in processing of sound at short timescales.
source: Although careful selection of circumscribed lesions has the advantage of highlighting behavioral differences without confounding other deficits (e.g., primary auditory processing), it is possible that additional regions are involved in processing of sound at short timescales.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Tractography based on healthy participants makes it possible to indirectly obtain information (i.e., structural disconnection) about brain regions contributing to the investigated function.
source: However, tractography based on healthy participants makes it possible to indirectly obtain information (i.e., structural disconnection) about brain regions contributing to the investigated function.
evidence: This is a methodological justification.

claim: The small number of patients might hamper the ability to detect statistically significant differences between the behavior of controls and patients.
source: In addition, it is likely that the small number of patients might hamper the ability to detect statistically significant differences between the behavior of controls and patients.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The current results align with the fact that the posterior superior temporal cortex contributes to the processing of sound at short timescales, as indicated by previous neuropsychological evidence and lesion studies.
source: Nevertheless, we are confident that the current results align with the fact that the posterior superior temporal cortex contributes to the processing of sound at short timescales, as indicated by previous neuropsychological evidence and lesion studies (Boemio et al., 2005; Chedru et al., 1978; Efron, 1963; Robson et al., 2013; Swisher and Hirsh, 1972).
evidence: This is a statement of confidence based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: The results confirm the processing of sound at short timescales in the left STS in patients with left temporal lesions.
source: Second, although the results confirm the processing of sound at short timescales in the left STS in patients with left temporal lesions, we did not include a right hemisphere patient control group to test for lateralization.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Right hemisphere lesions tend to be more extensive and rarely spare the primary auditory cortex.
source: This would be problematic in the first place as right hemisphere lesions tend to be more extensive and rarely spare the primary auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a justification for not including a right hemisphere patient control group.

claim: A comparison of left and right temporal lesions would have been likely confounded by a primary auditory processing deficit.
source: While a comparison of left and right temporal lesions would have allowed distinguishing processing differences of shorter and longer timescales, such a comparison would have been likely confounded by a primary auditory processing deficit.
evidence: This is a justification for not including a right hemisphere patient control group.

claim: The study provides indirect measures of disconnection based on probabilistic tractography in healthy participants.
source: Third, we provide indirect measures of disconnection based on probabilistic tractography in healthy participants.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: Not only lesions in the pSTS but also the connected networks are associated with the processing of sound at short timescales.
source: Even though we did not directly measure differences in tract integrity in LG+ and LG− patients, we argue that not only lesions in the pSTS but also the connected networks are associated with the processing of sound at short timescales.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: This interpretation is valid because previous studies have confirmed that behavioral deficits are explained to a similar extent by both the local damage and indirectly measured disconnection.
source: We believe that this interpretation is valid because previous studies have confirmed that behavioral deficits are explained to a similar extent by both the local damage and indirectly measured disconnection (Salvalaggio et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a justification based on cited literature.

claim: The left posterior temporal cortex contributes to audition in a time-sensitive manner.
source: We show that the left posterior temporal cortex contributes to audition in a time-sensitive manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: These results provide compelling evidence for a mechanism that in its simplicity not only applies to audition but may extend to other modalities relying on similar structural connectivity patterns.
source: Taken together, these results provide compelling evidence for a mechanism that in its simplicity not only applies to audition but may extend to other modalities relying on similar structural connectivity patterns (visual motion perception [Sokolov et al., 2014]; multisensory integration [Baumann and Greenlee, 2007; Schmahmann and Pandya, 1991]).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: This points to a possible common neurobiological function supporting internal modeling of a dynamic environment.
source: This points to a possible common neurobiological function (Schmahmann, 2004) supporting internal modeling of a dynamic environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Left and right cerebellum contribute to the encoding of event boundaries across long and short timescales, respectively.
source: Left and right cerebellum contribute to the encoding of event boundaries across long (red) and short (blue) timescales, respectively (Callan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption based on cited literature.

claim: Event representations are extracted from salient modulations of sound properties, that is, changes in the speech envelope (fluctuations in overall amplitude) corresponding to syllables and the fine structure (formant frequency transitions) corresponding to phonemes.
source: These event representations are extracted from salient modulations of sound properties, that is, changes in the speech envelope (fluctuations in overall amplitude, red) corresponding to syllables (s1–s4) and the fine structure (formant frequency transitions, blue) corresponding to phonemes (e1–e4) (Rosen, 1992; Weise et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption based on cited literature.
